entries.claim: A limit-overrun or single-use business-logic claim is confirmed only when parallel requests to the same single-use endpoint succeed where an identical sequential sequence fails, proving the limit was overrun rather than merely exercised twice.
steps: Prove the sink reads a file at all BEFORE testing traversal: fetch a file you KNOW exists on the target and confirm real content comes back.
If you cannot get a known-good read, there is no traversal finding to report — the sink is not proven.
Then apply the traversal value and confirm the returned content is from OUTSIDE the intended directory. Content, not status code.
Reject any result where only the status line differs: proxies, error handlers and WAFs produce status differentials with no file ever read.
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — single: **do** one parser sees the request; **observe** a consistent rejection or acceptance.
- **What sits between client and sink?** — cached: **do** add a cache-buster, then repeat without; **observe** whether a cached 200 masked the real path.
- **What must be TRUE server-side for this to bite?** — warm: **do** repeat after a success; **observe** behaviour once a cached/derived artefact exists.
- **AS whom are you testing?** — low_priv: **do** send as your lowest-privilege account; **observe** whether the response differs from anonymous.
- **What PROVES it, beyond a status code?** — differential: **do** compare against a control that differs in one variable; **observe** the difference the control did not produce.

steps: Identify the check and the use as TWO separate operations, and measure the gap between them.
Fire many parallel attempts (tens to hundreds) so at least one lands inside the window.
Vary ONLY the timing; the payload and session stay fixed.
Report a rate, not a single success: N successes in M attempts both proves the window and tells the reader whether it is practical to exploit.

entries.claim: An endpoint that encrypts attacker-controlled input with the server's key and returns the ciphertext becomes an oracle whenever another endpoint accepts ciphertext under the same algorithm.
steps: Record the BASELINE: request the endpoint with a benign, known-good value for the parameter. Save the full response (status, length, body hash).
Change exactly ONE variable: set the parameter to the attack value. Send it again with identical method, headers and cookies.
DIFF the two responses on all three axes: status code, body length, and body content hash.
Attribute every difference. A difference the control did not produce is the finding; a difference the control also produces is the application's normal behaviour.
Then re-run the attack value THREE times to separate a real condition from per-request noise (timing, nonce, ordering).
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — single: **do** one parser sees the request; **observe** a consistent rejection or acceptance.
- **What PROVES it, beyond a status code?** — state: **do** read the state back; **observe** the change visible to a second identity.

entries.claim: To decide this case, observe: The lookalike: you submit an order with quantity 99 or a 90 percent discount field, the response body echoes your figure back in a price or total field, and it is filed as business-logic manipulation.
steps: Build the ladder BEFORE probing: raw, single-encoded, double-encoded, and over-long variants of the same logical value.
Send each rung with the baseline procedure (one variable changed).
Record which rung first produces an effect. That rung identifies the decoding layer the application applies, and where the check and the decode disagree.
Verify WHERE normalisation happened: reflect the value in a way only the server could compute. Client-side canonicalisation proves nothing about the server.
